 8th Pay Commission: Pensioners Renew a Demand Rejected by the 7th CPC and What It Would Mean for Pension, Family Pension and Gratuity
 Source: Shutterstock
 You are reading a free article with opinions that may differ from the recommendation given by Kalkine in its paid research reports. Become a Kalkine member today to get access to our research reports, in-depth technical and fundamental research. Learn More 
 Highlights 
 Pensioners have renewed a demand before the 8th Pay Commission to raise pension above 50% of last pay drawn.
 The Bharat Pensioners Samaj seeks a minimum pension of ₹45,000, pension at 67% of last pay and family pension at 50%.
 The 7th CPC examined and rejected the demand, saying pension was already liberalised.
 A higher pension rate would not change gratuity, which is not calculated on pension.
 The article's illustration for a Level 6 employee shows a monthly pension rising from ₹22,450 to ₹30,083.
 Where the Demand Stands
 A demand to raise pension above 50% of last pay drawn was first placed before the 7th Central Pay Commission, which recorded and examined it and then turned it down. It is now before the 8th Pay Commission through a memorandum from the Bharat Pensioners Samaj. The 7th Commission noted that some parties questioned the basis for setting pension at 50% of last pay, and that it had received representations to raise family pension from 30% to 50%.
 The 6th Commission had set pension at 50% of last pay or the average emoluments of the last ten months, whichever was more beneficial, and had removed the 33-year qualifying service requirement. The 7th Commission said the pension arrangement had already been liberalised and that its pay recommendations would raise last pay and therefore pension, so it recommended no further increase in the pension or family pension rate.
 What the Pensioners Are Asking For
 The Bharat Pensioners Samaj seeks three linked measures: a minimum pension of ₹45,000, pension at 67% of last pay drawn and family pension at 50% of last pay drawn. The ₹45,000 minimum is sought because a percentage increase alone would do little for the lowest pensions.
 Illustration for a Level 6 Employee
 The source illustrates the effect for a Level 6 employee with last basic pay of ₹44,900, excluding dearness relief and other allowances. At 50%, monthly pension is ₹22,450 and annual pension ₹2,69,400. At 67%, monthly pension is ₹30,083 and annual pension ₹3,60,996, a difference of ₹7,633 a month and ₹91,596 a year. Family pension at 30% is ₹13,470 and at 50% is ₹22,450, a difference of ₹8,980.
 The 67% rate is 34% more than 50%, and the percentage change is the same for all pensioners while the rupee gain scales with last pay. In the source's examples, a Level 1 retiree on ₹18,000 would gain ₹3,060 a month and a Level 12 retiree on ₹78,800 would gain ₹13,396 a month. These are illustrations of the demand and not decisions.
 Family Pension
 The 7th Commission kept family pension at 30% of last pay. If both demands were accepted, family pensioner payouts would rise by about two-thirds. Under the 7th Commission's rules, enhanced family pension is payable for ten years from the date of death for death in service, with no upper age limit, and for seven years or until age 67, whichever is less, for death after retirement. The 7th Commission declined to extend the second period to ten years.
 Gratuity
 A higher pension rate does not increase gratuity, because gratuity is not calculated on pension. Gratuity equals one-fourth of emoluments for each completed six-month period of qualifying service, capped at 16.5 times last emoluments. The ceiling was raised from ₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh, is indexed to rise by 25% whenever dearness allowance rises by 50%, and has since been increased to ₹25 lakh according to the source. For the Level 6 example with dearness allowance at 63%, gratuity is about ₹12.08 lakh, which is below the ceiling, and only a pay revision that raises emoluments would change it.
 Cost and Outlook
 A 34% increase in pension for all civil pensioners would be costly, since pensions are among the government's largest revenue commitments. The 7th Commission's position was that pensioners benefit through pay revisions, while the pensioners' response is the ₹45,000 floor. It remains to be seen whether the 8th Commission will choose proportional rewards for long service, a fixed minimum pension for the lowest paid, or both.
 Conclusion
 The renewed demand puts the basis of the pension rate back before a pay commission, with potential effects on pension, family pension and, indirectly, retirement planning for central government employees. The 8th Pay Commission has not decided on the demand, and the figures above are illustrations of what it would mean if accepted.
 FAQs
 Q: What are pensioners asking the 8th Pay Commission for? 
 A: A minimum pension of ₹45,000, pension at 67% of last pay drawn and family pension at 50% of last pay drawn.
 Q: Why did the 7th CPC reject the demand? 
 A: It said pension had already been liberalised and that its pay recommendations would raise last pay and therefore pension.
 Q: What is the Level 6 illustration? 
 A: For last basic pay of ₹44,900, monthly pension would rise from ₹22,450 at 50% to ₹30,083 at 67%, excluding dearness relief.
 Q: Would gratuity increase with a higher pension rate? 
 A: No. Gratuity is not calculated on pension, so only a pay revision raising emoluments would change it.
 Q: Has the 8th Pay Commission accepted the demand? 
 A: No. The demand is before the Commission, and the source says it remains to be seen how it will respond.
